turns.question: what would my pension be if I retired now?
turns.answer:
**Calculated, with assumptions**

If you retired on 2026-09-13, your estimated pension would be $32,126.78 a year ($2,677.23 a month). This estimate assumes your annuity begins at age 56.

| If you retire | Years of service | Annual pension | Monthly pension |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| retire now | 21.5 | $32,126.78 | $2,677.23 |

The 11-134(a) formula used here is a statutory election. The Code lets you choose it instead of another employee annuity under that section; on your numbers, the figure shown is the larger option. [40 ILCS 5/11-134]

**What I assumed**

- the date you stop working, taken as today

**Worth knowing**

- You reach age 60 in 44 months. Waiting until then is worth about $10,130.33 a year more than stopping now [40 ILCS 5/11-134].

Waiting gains you no increase in the comparison shown: the annual difference is $0.00 and the monthly difference is $0.00.

The projection holds the salary basis constant, carried forward at today’s level, and assumes continuous employment to that age.

Section 11-134(f-1) does not apply because its elected annuity must begin no earlier than age 60. Section 11-131 does not apply because it concerns withdrawal before age 55 followed by reaching age 55. Section 11-164(1) concerns refunds for withdrawal before age 55 or, with less than 10 years of service, withdrawal before age 60. Section 11-130 does apply, but the Pension Code does not contain the conversion factors needed to put a figure on its age-and-service annuity. [40 ILCS 5/11-134]

This is an estimate — your retirement fund makes the binding determination.

The age-and-service annuity in this provision is based on accumulated contributions, and the Pension Code does not set out the conversion factors needed to work that out.
This provision applies when an employee withdraws before age 55 and later attains age 55.

**How that is worked out**

| Step | Amount |
|---|---:|
| Withdrawal date | 2026-09-13 |
| Age at annuity start | 56 |
| Years of service | 21.5 |
| Highest average salary (best 4 years) | $69,956.40 |
| Months before age 60 | 44 |
| Age 60 | 60 |
| Minimum service years | 20 |
| Maximum salary percentage | 80.00% |
| Withdrawal effective date | $1,990.00 |
| Annual service accrual rate | 2.40% |
| Minimum annuity commencement age | 55 |
| Monthly early retirement reduction rate | 0.25% |
| Unreduced annuity | $36,097.50 |
| Early retirement reduction amount | $0.11 |
| Early retirement reduction factor | 0.89 |
| Reduced annuity | $32,126.78 |
| Statutory maximum annuity | $55,965.12 |
| Annual annuity | $32,126.78 |
| **Annual pension** | **$32,126.78** |
| **Monthly pension** | **$2,677.23** |

The calculation uses the Article 11(a) formula for an employee who withdraws on or after July 1, 1990, has 20 or more years of service, and begins the annuity no earlier than age 55. The Code provides a 2.40% service rate for withdrawal on or after January 1, 2002, with a 0.25% reduction for each month the annuity begins before age 60. [40 ILCS 5/11-134]

**What I assumed**

- the date you stop working, taken as today

**Worth knowing**

- You reach age 60 in 44 months. Waiting until then is worth about $10,130.33 a year more than stopping now [40 ILCS 5/11-134].

<<<alternatives>>>

Section 11-134(a) also gives you a choice of a tiered formula using 1.80%, 2.00%, 2.20%, and 2.40% for successive service periods. The figure shown is the larger option on your numbers. [40 ILCS 5/11-134]

Section 11-134(f-1) does not apply because that election requires the annuity to begin no earlier than age 60. [40 ILCS 5/11-134]

Section 11-130 applies because its age-and-service annuity is based on accumulated contributions, but the Pension Code does not contain the conversion factors needed to put a figure on it.

Section 11-131 does not apply because it concerns withdrawal before age 55 followed by later attainment of age 55.

Section 11-164(1) does not apply because it governs refunds for withdrawal before age 55 or, with less than 10 years of service, withdrawal before age 60.

This is an estimate — your retirement fund makes the binding determination.
